questions.stem: A monopoly is best defined as a market in which

options.text: a single firm supplies a commodity that has no close substitute
a few large firms supply the bulk of the market's output
many firms sell slightly differentiated products
there is only one buyer of a commodity

questions.explanation: Monopoly means one seller. The absence of a close substitute is just as important as the single seller, because if buyers could easily switch to another product the firm would have no real control over price.

distractorRationale.b: A few large firms dominating the market is oligopoly, not monopoly
distractorRationale.c: Many firms selling differentiated products describes monopolistic competition
distractorRationale.d: A single buyer is called a monopsony, which is a different concept

questions.stem: For a monopolist, the marginal revenue curve

options.text: lies above the average revenue curve
lies below the average revenue curve
coincides with the average revenue curve
is horizontal at the ruling market price

questions.explanation: To sell an extra unit the monopolist must cut price on every unit, not just the last one. The revenue gained from the extra unit is therefore reduced by the revenue lost on all the earlier units, so marginal revenue falls faster than price and lies below it.

distractorRationale.a: Marginal revenue can only exceed average revenue if price were rising as output rose, which contradicts the law of demand
distractorRationale.c: MR equals AR only when price is constant, which is the case of a price taker
distractorRationale.d: A horizontal MR curve belongs to perfect competition, where the firm faces a fixed price

questions.stem: A monopolist sells 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 units at prices of ₦100, ₦90, ₦80, ₦70 and ₦60 respectively. What is the marginal revenue, in naira, of the third unit?
questions.explanation: Total revenue at 2 units is 2 × ₦90 = ₦180 and at 3 units it is 3 × ₦80 = ₦240. Marginal revenue is the change in total revenue, ₦240 − ₦180 = ₦60. Notice this is less than the ₦80 price, because the price cut of ₦10 also applied to the two units already being sold.

questions.stem: Price discrimination by a monopolist is possible only if

options.text: the markets can be kept separate and have different elasticities of demand
the cost of producing the good differs between the two markets
the firm faces a horizontal demand curve
all buyers have identical incomes and tastes

questions.explanation: Separation stops buyers in the cheap market from reselling into the dear one, and different elasticities are what make two different prices worth charging — the higher price is loaded onto the market whose demand is more inelastic.

distractorRationale.b: If costs genuinely differ, charging different prices is not discrimination at all but simply cost-based pricing
distractorRationale.c: A horizontal demand curve means the firm is a price taker, which rules out discrimination completely
distractorRationale.d: Identical buyers would give identical elasticities, removing the very reason to discriminate

questions.stem: The supply of piped water to a city is usually left to one company because

options.text: water is not a scarce commodity
duplicating the pipe network would raise average cost enormously, making it a natural monopoly
the law forbids more than one company from selling any good
consumers prefer to buy from a government agency

questions.explanation: A natural monopoly arises where the fixed cost of the network is so large that one supplier serving the whole market produces at a much lower average cost than two suppliers each serving half. Laying a second set of pipes down every street would waste resources.

distractorRationale.a: Clean piped water is very scarce, which is precisely why its supply matters
distractorRationale.c: There is no such general law; monopoly is the exception, not the rule
distractorRationale.d: Consumer preference for a government agency is not the economic reason, and many water utilities are private

questions.stem: Which THREE of the following are measures a government can use to control monopoly?

options.text: Imposing a maximum price on the monopolist's product
Granting the monopolist a longer patent
Levying a tax on the monopolist's excess profit
Removing barriers to entry so that rivals can enter
Buying up all competing firms on the monopolist's behalf

questions.explanation: Price control caps exploitation directly, taxing excess profit transfers monopoly gains to the public, and removing entry barriers restores the competitive pressure that keeps price near cost. All three attack either the monopolist's price, its profit or its protection.

distractorRationale.b: A longer patent extends the legal barrier to entry and so strengthens monopoly power
distractorRationale.e: Buying up rivals is amalgamation, one of the ways monopolies are created in the first place

questions.stem: A monopolist can continue to earn abnormal profit in the long run.
questions.explanation: True. Long-run profits are competed away only when new firms are free to enter. Barriers to entry are the defining feature of monopoly, so there is no mechanism to erode the abnormal profit and it can persist indefinitely.

distractorRationale.b: This confuses monopoly with perfect competition, where free entry drives long-run profit down to normal profit

questions.stem: Outline three sources of monopoly power and explain two disadvantages of monopoly to the consumer.
markingGuide: Legal grant: a patent, copyright or Act of parliament gives one firm the exclusive right to supply, as with the Central Bank of Nigeria's sole right to issue currency (2 marks)
Natural monopoly: a single large network such as water pipes or electricity transmission lines is far cheaper than duplicating it (2 marks)
Any one of: control of a scarce raw material, a very large capital requirement, superior secret technology, or amalgamation of all rivals (2 marks)
Disadvantage: output is restricted and price is set above marginal cost, so consumers pay more and consume less than under competition (2 marks)
Disadvantage: with no rival to fear, the monopolist may let quality and service fall, and consumers have no alternative supplier to turn to (2 marks)
questions.explanation: A full answer names the source of the barrier in each case rather than simply asserting that the firm is large. On the consumer side, the two strongest points are restricted output at a price above marginal cost, and the loss of quality and choice that follows from the absence of rivalry. Mentioning price discrimination against inelastic buyers earns credit too.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a monopoly?
questions.explanation: A monopoly is characterized by a single seller and high barriers to entry, resulting in no close substitutes for the product. Therefore, the presence of many close substitutes contradicts the definition of a monopoly.

distractorRationale.a: This is a key feature of monopoly.
distractorRationale.b: Monopolists have the power to set prices due to lack of competition.
distractorRationale.d: High barriers to entry prevent other firms from entering the market.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a source of monopoly power?
questions.explanation: Government regulation can create monopolies by granting exclusive rights to a single firm, effectively eliminating competition. This is a significant source of monopoly power.

distractorRationale.b: Perfect competition does not lead to monopoly power.
distractorRationale.c: Consumer preferences can influence demand but do not create monopoly power by themselves.
distractorRationale.d: Market surplus does not relate to monopoly power.

questions.stem: What is price discrimination?

options.text: Charging different prices to different customers for the same product
Setting a uniform price for all customers

questions.explanation: Price discrimination involves charging different prices to different customers for the same product based on their willingness to pay. This practice allows monopolists to maximize profits.

distractorRationale.b: A uniform price does not reflect price discrimination.
distractorRationale.c: Discounts are not the same as price discrimination, which is based on customer segmentation.
distractorRationale.d: Selling below cost is not a form of price discrimination.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions is necessary for a monopolist to successfully practice price discrimination?
questions.explanation: To successfully implement price discrimination, a monopolist must be able to segment the market and charge different prices based on each segment's willingness to pay. This segmentation is crucial for maximizing profits.

distractorRationale.b: Close substitutes would reduce the effectiveness of price discrimination.
distractorRationale.c: Perfect information is not required for price discrimination.
distractorRationale.d: Unequal demand is actually a prerequisite for price discrimination.

questions.explanation: Governments can control monopolies by implementing antitrust laws that prohibit anti-competitive practices and promote competition within the market. This helps to protect consumers and ensure fair pricing.

distractorRationale.a: Encouraging mergers can lead to more monopolistic behavior.
distractorRationale.c: Reducing taxes does not control monopolies effectively.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a natural monopoly?
questions.explanation: Electricity supply is an example of a natural monopoly because the infrastructure costs are so high that it is more efficient for a single provider to serve the entire market rather than having multiple competing firms.

distractorRationale.a: A local bakery operates in a competitive market.
distractorRationale.c: Clothing retail is also competitive with many players.
distractorRationale.d: Grocery stores face competition from various other stores.

options.text: Different prices based on consumer segments

questions.explanation: Price discrimination is characterized by charging different prices to different consumer segments based on their willingness to pay, allowing monopolists to maximize profits.

distractorRationale.a: Charging the same price contradicts the concept of price discrimination.
distractorRationale.c: Market segmentation is essential for price discrimination.
distractorRationale.d: Equal demand would negate the need for price discrimination.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a feature of monopoly power?

options.text: Many firms compete in the market
A single seller dominates the market
Easy entry and exit in the market

questions.explanation: A monopoly is characterized by a single seller who controls the entire market for a particular good or service. This means that there are no close substitutes available, allowing the monopolist to set prices without competition.

distractorRationale.a: This describes perfect competition, not monopoly.
distractorRationale.c: Homogeneous products are typical in perfect competition, not monopoly.
distractorRationale.d: Monopolies face high barriers to entry, making it difficult for new firms to enter.

distractorRationale.a: Different elasticities are essential for effective price discrimination.
distractorRationale.b: Market segmentation is crucial for identifying different consumer groups.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about price discrimination is true?

options.text: It is illegal in all markets
It requires market power to be effective
It leads to a single price for all consumers

questions.explanation: Price discrimination requires a firm to have market power to set different prices for different consumers based on their willingness to pay. Without market power, a firm cannot effectively discriminate prices.

distractorRationale.a: Price discrimination is legal in many markets, depending on regulations.
distractorRationale.b: Not all consumers benefit equally; some may pay more than others.
distractorRationale.d: Price discrimination results in multiple prices, not a single price.

questions.stem: One major barrier to entry in a monopoly is:

distractorRationale.a: Low startup costs would encourage entry, not serve as a barrier.
distractorRationale.c: High competition is characteristic of competitive markets, not monopolies.
distractorRationale.d: Consumer loyalty typically favors established monopolists rather than new entrants.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of price discrimination?

options.text: Charging different prices for the same product based on location
Offering a discount for bulk purchases
Setting the same price for all consumers

questions.explanation: Charging different prices for the same product based on location is a classic example of price discrimination, as it reflects varying consumer willingness to pay in different markets.

distractorRationale.b: Discounts for bulk purchases are not price discrimination as they apply to all buyers who meet the criteria.
distractorRationale.c: Setting the same price for all consumers does not constitute price discrimination.
distractorRationale.d: Increasing prices during a sale is not related to price discrimination.

questions.explanation: Natural monopolies typically arise in industries where high fixed costs and low marginal costs make it inefficient for multiple firms to operate, leading to a single provider being more efficient.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes price discrimination?

options.text: Charging different prices to different consumers for the same product
Setting a single price for all consumers
Increasing prices for all consumers uniformly

questions.explanation: Price discrimination occurs when a seller charges different prices to different consumers for the same good or service, based on their willingness to pay. This practice can help maximize profits for monopolists by capturing consumer surplus.

distractorRationale.c: Offering discounts to all consumers does not differentiate between consumer segments, hence it's not price discrimination.
distractorRationale.d: Increasing prices uniformly does not reflect the practice of charging different prices based on consumer segments.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a condition that must be met for effective price discrimination?

options.text: The seller must be a price taker
The seller must be able to segment the market
The product must have close substitutes

questions.explanation: For effective price discrimination, the seller must be able to segment the market based on different consumer characteristics or willingness to pay. This allows the monopolist to charge varying prices effectively.

distractorRationale.a: Identical demand among consumers contradicts the need for price discrimination.
distractorRationale.b: A price taker cannot set prices, which is essential for price discrimination.
distractorRationale.d: Close substitutes would limit a monopolist's ability to charge different prices.

questions.stem: What is a primary source of monopoly power?
questions.explanation: Control of a unique resource is a primary source of monopoly power, as it allows a firm to dominate the market without competition. This unique control creates significant barriers for other firms seeking to enter the market.

distractorRationale.a: Government regulation can sometimes limit monopolies rather than create them.
distractorRationale.b: High competition typically leads to lower prices and reduced monopoly power.
distractorRationale.d: Low barriers to entry facilitate competition, which is contrary to monopoly power.
